job: Fresh graduate in business, finance and accounting
name: Fatima Okafor

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and what you really think. Tell me about a normal day right now.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm in the office by 9 at Ledgerly, a small fintech that does tax and bookkeeping for freelancers. I'm a junior tax associate, and I do the first review of client returns with an AI assistant open on the left half of my screen. I finished my accounting and finance degree top of my class in the summer, after internships at an accountancy firm and a bank. I share a flat with my cousin Adaeze, and on weekends I help my dad in his pharmacy with the stock sheets. He still counts boxes by hand, which drives me a little mad.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let me read the first picture, called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say good, the tools are a bit better, and I'm already making use of them every day. At work I'd tell my team lead Rohan that it's a sensible nudge, not a revolution. Online I'd roll my eyes at the people who said it would end all jobs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I'm fine. I already do half my first-pass reviews with an assistant, and Rohan still signs off on every return that matters. The tool is faster, but a person still has to answer to the tax office.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep going and keep using the AI to get quicker, then use the saved time to take on harder client files. I'd start my professional tax qualification this spring. I'd also sort out my dad's stock sheets with a simple spreadsheet, to practise.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Comfortable. I like being the person who knows how the tools work, and I get a bit of pride out of it. There's no knot in my stomach.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which bill or worry in your own life would stay exactly the same even if nothing changed?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My student loan, about £110 a month, and helping my parents with the pharmacy's slow months. Dad sometimes asks me for a loan when a supplier is late. That worry is always there.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How much of your week is routine screen work that even a small change could touch?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Most of it, honestly. Maybe 70 percent of my day is tax forms and checks, and the assistant already helps with the dull parts. Even in a hype-free world I'd expect the firm to need fewer people for the same clients, which is why I try to stay ahead.

say: I'd tell my team lead it's a **sensible nudge**, not a revolution.
I'd say the doom talk about every job vanishing was **overblown**.
I'd tell friends to use the tools, because they're **useful**.
think: I'm fine, since a **person** still answers to the tax office.
I do half my first reviews with an assistant, so I'm already **ahead**.
I worry about my **dad's** pharmacy cash flow, not my own job.
do: Keep using the AI to get **faster**, then take harder client files.
Start my professional **tax** qualification this spring.
Build my dad a simple **stock** spreadsheet for his pharmacy.
feel: **Comfortable**, and proud of being the one who knows the tools.
S0.quote: I already do half my first-pass reviews with an assistant, and Rohan still signs off on every return that matters.
fieldNote: Her calm is based on **daily use** of AI tools, not on ignorance of them.
Her worries are about **family** cash flow, not her own job.
Volunteered that 70 percent of her day is **screen work**.

steps.text: Use the assistant on every first-pass tax review
Start the professional tax qualification this spring
Take on two harder client files a month

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let me read the next one, called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At work I'd say it's coming and that the firm should decide now how we use it, rather than react later. Online I'd share how I use it and what to check, because I think people hide it. I'd also say we need rules so staff get a share of the productivity.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Personally I'm one of the lucky ones, I think, because I'm already using it every day. But the entry-level work I do is the work that shrinks. I've seen Rohan quietly stop asking for a second junior because the assistant covers the tax-return checks.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd spend the evenings on the new reporting tool and learn how to prompt it for client advice rather than just forms. I'd start a small tax newsletter for freelancers, as a side income and a way to become known. And I'd move toward the advisory side, where a client asks me a real question.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Excited and a bit competitive. There's some unease, I won't pretend there isn't, because the sensible entry route into this career is narrowing. But I like riding it rather than being flattened.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Think of a task you did last week. Which part would software take over first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The routine returns, the ones where a freelancer has three invoices and a mileage claim. The assistant can draft those now and in a year it will do them end to end. What stays is the call where a client asks what to do about a shaky year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would your manager do differently about hiring people at your level?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: They'd hire fewer juniors, and the ones they hire would be expected to do the work of two. They'd also push everyone to billing by outcome. I'd say the partners will like it and some staff will have to work harder to keep the same pay.

say: I'd say the firm should **decide now** how to use the tools.
I'd share how I use AI and **what to check**.
I'd say staff should get a share of the **productivity**.
think: I'm one of the **lucky ones** because I already use it every day.
Entry-level work like mine is what **shrinks**, and the entry route narrows.
I'd rather **ride** the change than be flattened.
do: Learn the new reporting tool and **prompt** it for client advice.
Start a small tax **newsletter** for freelancers as side income.
Move toward **advisory** work where clients ask real questions.
feel: Some **unease** that the career entry route is narrowing.
S1.quote: I've seen Rohan quietly stop asking for a second junior because the assistant covers the tax-return checks.
fieldNote: Sees that even **good users** of AI face fewer junior seats.
Her answer to risk is to climb into **advice**, not to hide.

steps.text: Learn the new reporting tool and use it for client advice
Write a monthly tax newsletter for freelancers
Ask Rohan to put me on advisory calls

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let me read the next one, called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a moment for governments to step in hard, with retraining and some kind of income floor. Companies need to be told to give notice and to share the gains. Online I'd be loud about it, because I don't think quiet is a good plan when it's two years away.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly I'd feel scared, even though I'm the sort who uses it well. If AI does almost any thinking job better and cheaper, being good with AI isn't a skill, it's the baseline. Being the person who is good at using the machine only helps until the machine doesn't need anyone to use it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd save hard, aiming for six months of costs, and start a side business straight away, like tax help for freelancers using the tools. I'd learn what physical or relationship-heavy work needs people, perhaps healthcare finance, since my dad's pharmacy shows how much is local and face to face. I'd also be clear with my cousin Adaeze that we need a cheaper flat.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alert and a little dizzy. It's the first one where my own plan doesn't really protect me. I'd feel thrilled and terrified in the same hour.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Say it's the day the announcement is made. What do you tell the people close to you that night?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my parents that night to keep their savings liquid and not to expand the pharmacy. Dad would say a pharmacy always has customers, and I'd say yes, but the supply side may change. I'd offer to put in what I can.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: With only 2 years, what happens to the money you owe and the money you've saved?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stop paying extra on my student loan and keep cash, since I'd rather owe than be broke. I'd also spend some on a short course in something that needs trust, like financial planning, so I have a credential and not just AI skills.

say: I'd say governments must step in with **retraining** and an income floor.
I'd say firms should give **notice** and share the gains.
I'd be loud online, because **quiet** is no plan.
think: Even an AI power-user is **scared**, since using the machine becomes baseline.
My own plan doesn't really **protect** me here.
Face-to-face work like my dad's **pharmacy** may last longer.
do: Save six months of costs and start a **freelancer tax** side business.
Study a trust-based field like **financial planning**.
Tell Adaeze we need a **cheaper** flat.
feel: **Dizzy**, thrilled and terrified in the same hour.
**Alert**, with no sense of being protected.
S2.quote: Being the person who is good at using the machine only helps until the machine doesn't need anyone to use it.
fieldNote: A skilled **AI user** still feels exposed once AI outruns users.
Reaches for **trust-based** work and her dad's local trade.
Wants **cash** over paying down the loan.

steps.text: Save six months of costs before 2028
Sell tax help to freelancers on weekends
Study for a financial planning certificate
Move with Adaeze to a cheaper flat

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let me read the next one, called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is long enough to do something, but only if companies and governments start now. I'd push for training budgets and a say for staff in how AI is rolled out. And I'd tell friends to build something they own, not just a job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I'd feel better than with two years. By 2031 I'd be 27 with five years of experience and a side business. Five years is long enough to own something, a newsletter or a small practice, instead of just renting out my hours.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish my tax qualification and then start the planning one. I'd grow the freelancer practice until it earns real money, test new tools as they come, and save about £400 a month. I'd also spend one weekend a month helping my dad's pharmacy with its systems.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Excited with an edge. I like that I can act, and I'm irritated that so many people around me are not.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What changes about your plan with 5 years instead of 2?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd look at a long game. With two years I'd stack cash and exits. With five I'd build assets and a name, because a reputation is something an AI doesn't take from you quickly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who around you do you think sees this coming, and who doesn't?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My bosses mostly don't see it. The tax partners think the tools are a nicer calculator. The people who do see it are my friends who work in data, and my cousin, who has already switched courses.

say: I'd say five years is long enough, **if** companies start now.
I'd push for **training budgets** and staff say in rollouts.
I'd tell friends to build something they **own**.
think: With five years I'd have experience and a **side business**.
Owning something beats **renting out** my hours.
A **reputation** is hard for AI to take quickly.
do: Finish my tax qualification, then start the **planning** one.
Grow the freelancer **practice** and save £400 a month.
Spend a weekend a month on my dad's **pharmacy** systems.
feel: **Irritated** that many around me aren't acting.
S3.quote: Five years is long enough to own something, a newsletter or a small practice, instead of just renting out my hours.
fieldNote: Time makes her think about **assets and reputation**.
Impatient with **older** colleagues who miss the shift.
Her family **pharmacy** keeps coming up as her anchor.

steps.text: Pass the tax qualification, then start the planning one
Grow the freelancer practice to ten regular clients
Trial each new AI tool at work within a month

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let me read the next one, called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is enough to rebuild how we train people, and that the unions and schools need to start now. I'd say it's an opportunity if the gains are shared and a mess if they aren't. I'd also say the worry about robots is for later.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd feel fairly good. By 2036 I'd be 32, probably running my own small practice or part of a team that blends advice and tools. I think I'm built for change, but I'd still worry about who's left behind.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd build the practice step by step and invest in an index fund every month. I'd learn the planning side and maybe a short coding course. And I'd help my dad move the pharmacy onto a better stock system, as a test of what I can build.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Positive. A bit of nerves, but mostly curiosity. I like the idea of being one of the people who writes the rules for how this is used.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: With a decade, what would you start now that you wouldn't with 2 years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd also get involved in a professional body or a local policy group on skills. With ten years I can afford to care about more than my own pay. I'd want the next graduates to have an entry route.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: At 32, what do you hope your working life looks like, and what could stop that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At 32 I'd like to run a small practice with two or three juniors who learn properly, but a client base needing no human at all could stop that. I'd also worry about a recession making firms scrap training.

say: I'd say it's an **opportunity** if gains are shared and a mess if not.
I'd say unions and schools should **start now**.
I'd say the robot worry is for **later**.
think: By 2036 I'd be 32 and perhaps running my own **practice**.
I'm built for change, but still worry about those **left behind**.
I'd like to help write the **rules** for use.
do: Invest in an **index fund** each month.
Move my dad's pharmacy onto a better **stock system**.
S4.quote: At 32 I'd like to run a small practice with two or three juniors who learn properly, but a client base needing no human at all could stop that.
fieldNote: She can afford **wider** concerns once there's time.
Wants **entry routes** for later graduates, which a calm outlook does not hide.
Her dad's pharmacy is a **test bed** for her skills.

steps.text: Invest £150 a month in an index fund
Grow the freelancer practice into a small firm
Set up a digital stock system for dad's pharmacy
Join a local skills policy group in my town

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, mostly because it leaves no time. What would help is retraining that's paid for, rules that make firms give notice, and some kind of income floor so people can retrain without losing everything. I'd also want my parents' pharmacy to be protected from the sudden shocks.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: I'd say I'm optimistic about my own life and angry about the system. Using AI well is not a plan on its own, because the plan has to include the people who can't use it. That's the bit most of my colleagues skip.

headlineQuote: Using AI well is not a plan on its own, because the plan has to include the people who can't use it.
portrait: Fatima is a **22-year-old** junior tax associate at a small fintech, top of her class, who uses AI tools every day.
She's curious and comfortable with risk, and builds a **side business** whenever she feels threatened.
She is progressive, blames short-term **corporate greed**, and wants rules and a share of the gains.
She is calm when change is slow, **anxious** at two years, and anchored by her family's pharmacy.
biggestWorry: The **2028** scenario, because being good with AI stops mattering and there's no time to prepare.
whatWouldHelp: Paid **retraining**, notice rules for firms, and an income floor so people can retrain safely.
